title: UK prosecutors file for extradition of the Tate brothers from the US
description: Prosecutors in the UK have lodged a formal request for the extradition of brothers Andrew and Tristan Tate from the US to face charges of rape and sex
body: Prosecutors in the UK have lodged a formal request for the extradition of brothers Andrew and Tristan Tate from the US to face charges of rape and sex trafficking.The US State Department, which received the requests last week, will review the extradition applications to make sure they comply with the existing agreement between the US and UK.But the lawyer for the brothers, who are dual US-UK citizens, accused British authorities of failing to provide the necessary supporting documents in the request.The brothers are facing a total of 59 charges in the UK, including rape and counts relating to sex trafficking and indecent images of a child. Both men deny any wrongdoing.The Crown Prosecution Service originally brought 21 charges, but added 38 more in July for alleged actions spanning between 2010 and 2017.US authorities took the men into custody in July after the UK announced the new charges. The brothers lost a bid to be released from a Florida jail on bail last week. UK authorities had until Wednesday 16 September to submit a full extradition request. Joe McBride, the brothers' lawyer, said he would be challenging the requests, arguing they were not backed up by the information needed under the extradition agreement.In a statement to the BBC, McBride said the brothers had also not received the extradition requests themselves, nor documents such as "a warrant, a charging document, and information that provides a reasonable basis to believe my clients committed these offences"."This cloak-and-dagger act speaks to the deception behind these accusations and to their weakness," he added.Once the State Department completes it review, there are still several legal steps before extradition can be permitted. Applications must go through the US Justice Department which will in turn forward it to the court, where the final decision on their extradition will be made.During this legal process, the Tate brothers will remain in jail in the US. An official letter from the State Department details that Andrew Tate, 39, is "wanted to stand trial in the United Kingdom" on a series of charges, including 10 counts of rape, three counts of arranging or facilitating trafficking for sexual exploitation and three counts of assault occasioning actual bodily harm.He is also accused of making and distributing indecent images of a child and possessing extreme pornography.Charges levelled against Tristan Tate, 38, include five counts of rape, six counts of assault occasioning actual bodily harm, three counts of sex trafficking and a sexual assault.Both men deny any wrongdoing.In response to the formal request for extradition from the US, a Home Office spokesperson said: "As a matter of long-standing policy and practice, we do not routinely comment on individual cases."The former professional kickboxers turned divisive social media influencers hold dual US and British citizenship, and had primarily been living in Romania since 2017. They have been accused of promoting misogyny and toxic masculinity online, which has attracted a large following, particularly from young men. Andrew Tate, who is a self-proclaimed "misogynist", first rose to fame after a 2016 appearance on the British version of reality TV show Big Brother.The brothers also faced sex-trafficking charges in Romania in 2022, and were under a travel ban until they were allowed to come to the US in 2025.Both brothers have denied all charges and allegations.

schema.headline: UK prosecutors file for extradition of the Tate brothers from the US

title: Snapchat considering daily time limits for teenagers, boss tells BBC
description: The boss of Snapchat-parent Snap Inc says the firm would be "willing to implement" time limits for teens, following a call from Meta for it to take ac
body: The boss of Snapchat-parent Snap Inc says the firm would be "willing to implement" time limits for teens, following a call from Meta for it to take action.Evan Spiegel told the BBC in an interview at the company's California headquarters that setting a maximum amount of time that young users could spend on the app could be "an important step forward for the industry." His comments came as Snap revealed a slew of new features for its upcoming Specs glasses, which it said could connect to Apple iPhone and Mac devices.Meta has been pressuring other social media companies to join it in making platform changes it agreed to as part of a recent multi-billion dollar legal settlement with US states.Instagram and Facebook-parent Meta was facing allegations from Attorneys General for most US states who said the firm deliberately designed its apps to be addictive to young users.It agreed to pay $12.7bn and implement a two-hour daily limit for teen users across its platforms by default, in addition to muted notifications during school hours, blocks at night and other measures."I think it is an important step forward in the industry in terms of really identifying industry norms, and I think that would be beneficial overall," Spiegel told the BBC. "We've looked really thoughtfully at the terms."As part of Meta's August settlement, the company said it would implement even more stringent time limits and pay an additional $5.3bn if YouTube and TikTok follow suit. It has denied any wrongdoing as part of the deal, which will be paid over a 10-year period.Last month, a Meta spokesperson said it was hopeful that Snap would make similar platform changes as well.Meta, YouTube, TikTok and Snap have all faced a barrage of litigation alleging their apps have helped spawn a youth mental health crisis. Snap has also been accused of facilitating illegal drug sales.When asked about the idea of a default time limit, Spiegel said: "I think that's a really good example of something that that we'd be willing to implement."But Spiegel did not commit to a timeline on when Snap might take action. "That's something we've talked about internally," he said. "I don't have more to share today."He noted that Snap offers tools through its Family Center feature, which currently enables parents to track aspects of how their teens are using Snapchat."We want to figure out how we can be part of the solution," Spiegel added.YouTube-parent Google said it had no comment when asked if it planned to implement the measures in Meta's settlement. TikTok did not respond to the BBC's request for comment.Spiegel was talking to the BBC as Snapchat's parent Snap Inc announced new features for its upcoming Specs glasses.He said the smart eyewear would use AI to suggest things for people to do based on what the tech learns about their goals, relationships and routines. "Rather than the way that people use chatbots today where you constantly have to ask for stuff, Specs can understand what's important to you, and then offer recommendations or offer next steps," he said.Like other smart glasses, Specs will use AI to let people see digital elements overlaid onto the world.But the tech won't come cheap - retailing at $2,195 in the US and £1,995 in the UK."The target audience right now is early adopters of tech and developers as well as enterprise," Spiegel said.With the device, Snap aims to offer a middle ground between VR headsets like Meta's Quest 3 and lightweight AI smart glasses offered by rivals which look more like conventional glasses."We're creating a totally new category here," said Spiegel. "You have a really powerful computer that brings a lot of the immersive capability you see with VR, but they're also lightweight at just about 130 grams, so they're very wearable and they have these see-through lenses, so you can use them out in the world."Specs is Snap's most recent foray into the wearable tech, coming a decade after its short-lived Spectacles cost the company tens of millions of dollars.The device is also arriving as Meta is facing a significant backlash over its own smart glasses, which are estimated to be the most popular of the market.Some online derisively call them "pervert glasses" over how they have been used to secretly film women, with one person telling the BBC they were filmed leaving the beach, while another said they were told to pay to remove a video of them from the internet.Nevertheless, sales continue to rise. With seven million pairs having been sold according to Meta.Snap said it has built into the design of Specs, which do not use facial recognition to identify people.A white light flashes at the top of the glasses above the users nose when it is recording video and taking a photo.The company says that will let people nearby see that recording is happening.Users of Meta glasses have figured out ways to obscure components meant to indicate that a photo or video is being captured, including by tampering with the electronics in the device.Meta says it has remotely disabled the cameras on thousands of its devices on which tampering or destruction of the indicator light was detected.

schema.headline: Snapchat considering daily time limits for teenagers, boss tells BBC

title: Part-human part-mouse brain developed in science breakthrough
description: The aim of this ethically complicated breakthrough was to better understand the biology of brain disorders for which there are currently no effective
body: The aim of this ethically complicated breakthrough was to better understand the biology of brain disorders for which there are currently no effective treatments.Some conditions cannot be studied in a mouse, simply because rodents do not develop some of the brain disorders that we do. As lead researcher Prof Sergiu Pașca from Stanford University explained in a press conference, psychiatry has "one of the lowest success rates for clinical trials"."Even drugs that actually make it to clinical trial - that seem to be working really well in animal models - fail dramatically in clinic," he said in a press conference. "That tells us we're missing a lot of information about human biology and capturing that will be essential."The Stanford researchers said that, for some complex conditions, including epilepsy, autism and cerebral palsy, it has the potential to be "transformative".Pașca said: "Here we have a new model that allows us to actually capture aspects of human brain function in a way that has not been possible before."The human brain is made up of billions of cells, interconnected in millions of circuits, making it difficult to understand its development and what exactly is happening – at the cellular level - when things go wrong.While this research is not the first time human neurons have been implanted in laboratory rodents, external, these scientists took that approach to a new level.First, they genetically-engineered mice to develop almost none of their own cerebral cortex – that is the outer layer of the brain sometimes referred to as "grey matter". It handles higher-level thinking, memory and senses.The researchers then used skin cells taken from humans and "reprogrammed" them, so they grew into pieces of brain-like tissue. These are structures called organoids – they are not whole brains grown in dishes, more collections of connected, living cells.When these organoids were implanted into the mouse brain the cells divided and organised themselves into the animal's existing brain circuitry, connecting with the rest of the mouse's brain and spinal cord.The cortex of the implanted mice is not perfect - normal cortex forms organised, structured layers. And as neuroscientist Dr Ilary Allodi put it, scans of these human-mouse brains look "a bit messy".  After a few months though, the human cells started to look and function like the outer layer of the mouse's brain.About six months after the surgery, scientists put the mice through some basic behavioural tests  - observing them as they moved around a small table-top arena.Pașca said they performed "largely as [the normal] mice did"."They don't have any enhancement," he added.Dr Sarah Chan, a reader in bioethics at the University of Edinburgh who was not involved in this research, told BBC News there was "no indication that what's being created here are mice that can think like humans, or a human brain in a mouse body."But she said the study "prompts us to think about what it might mean when we start changing animal cognition"."How can we know what it's like to be one of these mice? And how do we take account of that in the ways that we treat laboratory animals," she added.Dr Ilary Allodi, a neuroscientist from St Andrews University, who was not involved in the research, said the work the scientists had done was "very impressive".In particular, Allodi pointed to the fact that cell types that are found only in human and other primate brains - not in the brains of mice – spontaneously formed in the implanted mice. "You're keeping the human program inside the mouse environment – like the mouse is an incubator," she told BBC News.These mice, which the researchers said are engineered and reared under strict ethical and welfare guidelines, will most likely be used in a small number of labs for studies of a few, very specific brain disorders. Prof James Ainge, a neuroscientist who is also at St Andrews University, pointed out that while the development was technically very impressive, these mice could be "of limited use".This, he said, was partly due to the "ethical issues of raising living human brain tissue in a mouse and what that would mean for the experience of the animal".Neuroscientists who study the human brain, Allodi pointed out, all struggle with the same limitations. "We try to understand human disease, and what we have is mice, cells that live on a plate, and neural networks on a computer."So this is a new avenue."

schema.headline: Part-human part-mouse brain developed in science breakthrough

title: Pakistan hospital fire: Report finds no fire alarms or sprinklers at neonatal unit where fire killed 14
description: For many inside the hospital on the morning of 26 August, the first warnings were shouts.Abdul Ghafoor was in a nearby ward with his mother, who was a
body: For many inside the hospital on the morning of 26 August, the first warnings were shouts.Abdul Ghafoor was in a nearby ward with his mother, who was a patient, when he heard someone warning that a fire had erupted. He went upstairs to see if he could help."The entire ward was filled with smoke, we could not see anything," he told the BBC.CCTV from the corridor outside shows how quickly the fire spread. According to the report, the first indication that something was wrong came at 06:38 when a nurse can be seen running from the ward to get help, returning 20 seconds later with a security guard.Another nurse, Razia Noreen, is then seen rushing into the ward, emerging seconds later with one of the babies who turned out to be the only one to survive.Within a minute, the report says, dense smoke had obscured the camera.Hivsa Walid, her newborn niece and sister-in-law were in the ward next door. Hours later she told the BBC that they had heard a loud commotion and then realised it was a fire when they saw smoke emerging from the unit where the babies were sleeping."In that moment, I couldn't understand what was going on. We just focused on getting downstairs and saving ourselves."On the day of the fire, authorities suggested the fire had started from a spark in the ward's air conditioner.The report agrees that this was the most probable source of the fire, due to an overheating electrical supply cable - although it remains unclear what exactly the electrical defect was.The fire then spread quickly, igniting plastics, equipment and bins. Several babies in the ward were on oxygen support, but the report says that while oxygen may have intensified the fire, there isn't evidence that it created a pathway for it to spread.The air conditioning units had undergone maintenance, but the report says this is not the same as a safety check. Back in 2018, the hospital's air conditioning units had been approved to be replaced and upgraded, but eight years later this hadn't happened.The report states that there was no functioning smoke detection, fire alarms or sprinkler system. It found no evidence that the staff in the unit had been trained or had ever rehearsed how to evacuate the ward of newborns, many of whom were premature or "medically fragile". It also found staff had not been trained on how to isolate the oxygen supply in the case of an emergency.Several people described chaos and confusion in the hospital."There should have been fire extinguishers and protocols, but no one was doing anything," Walid said. "Everyone was just running."Ghafoor said that he was part of a group of seven or eight who tried to find a way to relieve the thick smoke; they managed to break glass panels at the end of the corridor before firefighters arrived.The emergency services weren't notified about the fire until 06:54, the report says, nearly 20 minutes after it first began. It says the first rescue workers arrived at 07:01.Like the firefighter who spoke to the BBC, Ghafoor also said rescue staff struggled to get through some of the hospital's doors.At the time, the hospital's executive director had told BBC News that the door to the newborns' ward was not locked, but guarded, because of previous incidents of baby abductions from government hospitals.The report says that while "ordinary access restrictions may be legitimate for security purposes… they cannot render designated emergency routes inaccessible when needed."The report also found that the hospital had received previous warnings about fire risks. A month before, a fire had broken out at its nursing hostel, raising issues with smoke detection, alarms and general fire preparedness.It says that the hospital and its senior management "bear the principal institutional responsibility for failing to convert known risks, prior warnings and assigned duties into an effective safety system".Pakistan's prime minister has directed the inquiry's short-term measures to be implemented within the next three months and ordered fire safety audits of public and private offices and buildings.He has also suspended eight officials and asked for criminal proceedings to be initiated against them.

schema.headline: Pakistan hospital fire: Report finds no fire alarms or sprinklers at neonatal unit where fire killed 14

title: Carabao Cup draw: League Two Fleetwood will host Arsenal in fourth round
description: League Two Fleetwood Town will host Premier League champions Arsenal in the fourth round of the Carabao Cup.The Lancashire side reached this stage for
body: League Two Fleetwood Town will host Premier League champions Arsenal in the fourth round of the Carabao Cup.The Lancashire side reached this stage for the first time in their history with a 1-0 win over Sheffield United on Wednesday night.And their reward was a plum home tie against Mikel Arteta's men, who beat Ipswich Town 4-2 on Tuesday.Holders Manchester City will welcome Brighton to Etihad Stadium if they beat Norwich in Thursday's remaining tie, while Chelsea manager Xabi Alonso will visit his former side Liverpool after the Premier League rivals were drawn together.League One sides Bradford and Peterborough will play for a place in the quarter-finals after they defeated Leyton Orient and Barnsley respectively in the third round.The remaining fixtures are all Premier League affairs with Fulham hosting Crystal Palace, Bournemouth at home to Aston Villa, Brentford travelling to Sunderland and Everton welcoming Newcastle UnitedThe fourth round will take place during the week commencing 26 October.

schema.headline: Carabao Cup draw: League Two Fleetwood will host Arsenal in fourth round

title: 'My rent was higher than my student loan' - the booming cost of private halls
description: Despite it being beyond her budget, Lara accepted the offer because of the difficulty of finding student housing in Edinburgh.She said the cost hung o
body: Despite it being beyond her budget, Lara accepted the offer because of the difficulty of finding student housing in Edinburgh.She said the cost hung over much of her first year at university and she was "constantly stressing" about how much money she was having to put towards rent.To cover the shortfall, she worked 20 hours per week alongside her studies, a decision she says contributed to her failing her first-year exams."I was exhausted all the time," she said. "I just didn't have enough time to study.""I think when pricing student housing they need to be more realistic."It makes it so difficult for students like me who don't come from a super wealthy background to find an affordable place to live."The University of Edinburgh said it offered students good value, across a broad range of price points, with entry-level rents being well below the average.A spokesperson said: "We encourage students to select accommodation that aligns with their lifestyle preferences and budget throughout the application process." Across the UK, a total of 206,005 students told the Higher Education Statistics Agency (HESA) they lived in private-sector halls in 2024/25.This is up from 117,995 a decade earlier.The rate of increase is higher in Scotland, up from 5,500 in 2014/15 to 14,640 last year.The growth of PBSA has been particularly visible in Scotland's two largest cities.As of August 2026, Glasgow has 21,655 student beds with a further 18,213 in the development pipeline, meaning the city could host almost 40,000 student beds if all proposed schemes go ahead.Edinburgh has also seen rapid growth, with the supply of PBSA increasing by almost 60% over the past decade.A further 5,917 beds were in the development pipeline as of December 2025.Richard Ward, the head of research at student accommodation marketing website StuRents, said the average cost of privately-operated PBSA in Edinburgh and Glasgow is £268 and £243 per person per week (pppw) respectively.The national average (excluding London) is £191pppw.He said: "The rents you're having to charge are about £250 to £300 per week to make a scheme financially viable"The challenge for the sector is, at that price point, a lot of domestic students cannot afford that."According to industry experts, international students, who are often better able to afford higher rents, are a key part of the PBSA market.It's something Lara, from Kelso in the Borders, noticed in her accommodation too."A lot of people I was friends with through my accommodation were international students, so funding is very different," she said."I think for the most part, a lot of people didn't have as much of a struggle paying the rent, but I definitely know a few people who were in the same boat as I was."For many international students, however, PBSA offers reassurance that can be difficult to find in the private rental market.Saba, an international student from Pakistan who had planned to study in Glasgow, said they felt safer than trying to organise a flat from the other side of the world."I didn't really know where to start," she said. "Every country has different laws when it comes to properties and renting places."After missing out on university accommodation, she considered trying to find a property through a private landlord, however, she says she "encountered a bunch of scammers" during her search, including one man who asked for £500 upfront before sending videos of the property. "As an international student, I feel like you're vulnerable" she said "There are good and bad people everywhere and the bad lot try to take advantage of that."Data from StuRents suggests occupancy rates have fallen in both Edinburgh and Glasgow.According to figures from June 2026, about 49.7% of rooms in Glasgow had been booked for the upcoming academic year, in comparison to 81.8% of rooms at the same point in 2024.Similarly, Edinburgh figures suggest that 63.2% of rooms have been booked in the same period, down from 80.6% in 2024.Nationally, 59.1% of rooms had been booked for the upcoming year in June 2026, compared with 70.4% in 2024.StuRents' Richard Ward added that the sector had experienced a surge in demand from international and postgraduate students following the Covid pandemic.However, he said growth in international student numbers had slowed, while new accommodation continued to come onto the market, leading to lower occupancy rates.International student figures in Scotland have fallen for two years in a row, with a 5% drop most recently.The largest cohort of international students in Scotland come from China.Ward said: "The challenge for developers and investors entering into the student market is that from the point of an application being approved to the building actually being complete could be three years, for example."During that time the local market could have radically shifted."Because of this, Ward says that pipeline figures do not necessarily translate into completed developments."I'm not expecting, by all means, anywhere near the full pipeline to be delivered in any market, but equally in Glasgow and Edinburgh," he said.

schema.headline: 'My rent was higher than my student loan' - the booming cost of private halls

title: Man Utd 2-3 Brighton: Michael Carrick 'not bothered' by pressure after loss
description: Sir Alex Ferguson was St Mirren manager the last time Manchester United lost at Old Trafford having taken a 2-0 lead.That is the context to the shocki
body: Sir Alex Ferguson was St Mirren manager the last time Manchester United lost at Old Trafford having taken a 2-0 lead.That is the context to the shocking Carabao Cup third-round exit his old club suffered against Brighton on Wednesday.It is a period of time that encompasses the legendary Scot's dynasties at Aberdeen as well as United. The Class of '92 were in nappies when John Pratt scored the winner for Tottenham on 4 September 1976.After holding protests inside and outside the ground before Sunday's loss to 10-man Manchester City, United supporters made their feelings known about their latest embarrassment in three ways.Most fans simply left as the players embarked on their post-match lap of appreciation.Some of those who remained booed, as they had done when their side fell behind 21 minutes from time.By the time they approached the tunnel, close to United's 'singing section', supporters were asking Michael Carrick and his players 'what was that?'. Their wording was somewhat more colourful.It is not certain where 15-year-old JJ Gabriel was while all this was taking place, but nothing happened that would make him think he had got it wrong by turning his back on the club.Indeed, it is quite possible, probable indeed, that the promised senior debut would have been scrapped given the game situation - and the fact skipper Bruno Fernandes was among the experienced players introduced in the frantic final stages."Of course we can turn it around, we have got some really good players," said Carrick. "It feels bad because we haven't had a great week or two, or three weeks."Carrick's side have won twice this season, against newly promoted Ipswich at home after falling behind, and Azerbaijani champions Sabah FK in the Champions League. They have now lost on three occasions, more defeats than he experienced in 17 matches after replacing Ruben Amorim in January.He has been around Manchester United long enough to know the pressure losing runs can build."I don't feel under pressure," he said. "Either way, that doesn't bother me one bit."I understand what goes on outside and how the world works, but it doesn't bother me. What bothers me is winning games, having a good feeling around the place and a good feeling around the group to know we're moving in a good direction."The problem is it doesn't feel as though they are moving in a good direction. There were certainly not many positives to take from this mess.The obvious one was Shea Lacey, who marked his first senior start with a well-taken eighth-minute goal. It meant he became the first teenager to score on his first United start since Marcus Rashford in February 2016.Lacey was one of eight changes made by Carrick. Defensively, those changes were not a success.Diogo Dalot was one of the three players to keep their place. His form has deserted him. Noussair Mazraoui is the back-up left-back, which only heightens the debate over the wisdom not to buy one before the transfer window closed. Leny Yoro and Ayden Heaven looked like the inexperienced defenders they are. In midfield Manchester United were overrun.Yet again, Rashford threatened without managing a goal or an assist. He came closest to levelling when he sped beyond the Brighton defence, but his shot was saved by Jason Steele."The longer the game went, the more we had control," was the concise assessment of Brighton boss Fabian Hurzeler. "I thought we deserved to win."Carrick didn't dispute the assessment.His greatest sadness was for Lacey, who should have had his name in lights but instead was part of a team scuttling off the pitch to the sound of boos and harsher criticism."It's a shame that Shea's moment, such a great moment for him, for his family, his friends and the whole academy; to have an academy player come in and have a moment like that, gets a bit lost, unfortunately," said Carrick."It won't for him when things settle down but, as we sit here now, it feels that it was a long time ago."Carrick also addressed the JJ Gabriel situation."He's a young boy, he's 15, and for me, definitely, and from a club point of view, looking after our younger players, their welfare, their wellbeing, their exposure, we've got to be really conscious of that in this situation," he explained.But ultimately, for any manager, the assessment of their work comes through results."Being here toughens you up over a period of time," he said. "It depends how you deal with it. You've got to deal with it in a way where you can cope with it and you can bring out the best in yourself. However you do that, with your motivation and the confidence deep within yourself to know we can win football matches."We've gone out of the cup tonight, and the feeling around the place feels bigger than that. I'm honest enough to say that's how it feels. But it doesn't have to be like that. If we win football matches again, it can go in a different direction."Manchester United have one more game before the international break, at Fulham on Sunday.For the general wellbeing of the club, Carrick's team really need to win.Speaking on Sky Sports, former England midfielder Jamie Redknapp said he wasn't sure they will."Right now, they're miles off it," he said. "It doesn't matter how good the manager is, if you don't have the right players it makes it really difficult."There's a reason why the other managers have struggled. Sooner or later the pressure's always going to come on."This weekend becomes a huge game. He doesn't need another poor result, otherwise all of a sudden you're going into the international break and everyone's talking about you. The winners tonight are the players who didn't play."

schema.headline: Man Utd 2-3 Brighton: Michael Carrick 'not bothered' by pressure after loss

title: Charles said Diana would be forgotten 'soon enough', Earl Spencer claims in book
description: Buckingham Palace has responded after a claim by Earl Spencer, the brother of Diana, Princess of Wales, that King Charles said "we'll forget her soon
body: Buckingham Palace has responded after a claim by Earl Spencer, the brother of Diana, Princess of Wales, that King Charles said "we'll forget her soon enough" days after her death.Earl Spencer alleged the then-Prince of Wales subjected him to a "stream of anger" after he insisted Diana would not have wanted Princes William and Harry, then aged 15 and 12, to walk in her funeral procession.The claim was made in an extract from his upcoming memoir, published by the Daily Mail.A Palace spokesperson said: "While we do not comment on books as a matter of principle, His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss."Swan Song: Diana, My Sister is due to be published next week and is expected to be highly critical of the Royal Family. BBC News has not seen the book in full.In the first extract, external from it to be made public, Earl Spencer claims to have been informed by a senior Palace aide that the young princes would walk alongside Princess Diana's coffin, which he objected to.He claims to have received a phone call from Charles shortly after.Earl Spencer wrote in the book: "He [Charles] unleashed down the phone what I have always taken to be his pent-up contempt for Diana, and his horror that the world was so bowled over by her death. 'Rest assured,' he hissed, 'we'll forget her soon enough'."Earl Spencer's book about his sister seems set to open a very difficult time in the recent history of the Royal Family.The death of Diana, a hugely popular figure, in a car crash in 1997, had created a volatile atmosphere, in which the royals were accused of failing to show feeling and empathy, and had seemed out of touch with the public mood.Earl Spencer's emotional and defiant speech at her funeral added to that cloud of grievance hanging over Diana's untimely death.Prince Harry has previously said that walking behind his mother's coffin aged 12 was something no child "should be asked to do". In 2017, he told the BBC he didn't "have an opinion whether that was right or wrong", but "looking back on it", he was glad to have been part of the day.Earlier on Wednesday, it emerged that copies of Earl Spencer's unreleased book had been stolen from a truck in the Netherlands.BBC News understands four copies of the Dutch language edition were taken from a truck while it was en route from the Dutch publisher's printers to their warehouse.

schema.headline: Charles said Diana would be forgotten 'soon enough', Earl Spencer claims in book

title: Two Britons among three killed in Swiss Alps light aircraft crash
description: Two Britons are among three people killed in a plane crash in the Swiss Alps.The light aircraft crashed high in the mountains near the town of Leukerb
body: Two Britons are among three people killed in a plane crash in the Swiss Alps.The light aircraft crashed high in the mountains near the town of Leukerbad in the southern canton of Valais on Tuesday.The authorities said the Cirrus SR22T took off from Sion airport in the Rhône Valley and, for unknown reasons, collided with a mountain slope about 10 minutes later.Witnesses reported seeing a fire and smoke.Emergency teams from the Valais Rescue Organisation, police and firefighters were sent to the scene along with three helicopters. The Swiss Transportation Safety Board has started an investigation.  And the Valais Police and the Office of the Attorney General have launched a inquiry.Formal identification of the victims is under way.The Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO) confirmed it was "providing support to the families of two British nationals who died in Switzerland".It said officials were in contact with the local authorities."Our thoughts remain with the families during this difficult time," it added.

schema.headline: Two Britons among three killed in Swiss Alps light aircraft crash

title: Interest rates hold expected but Bank of England facing tough choices
description: The Bank uses interest rates to control inflation, which charts the rising cost of living. It aims to keep inflation at a target rate of 2%.However, o
body: The Bank uses interest rates to control inflation, which charts the rising cost of living. It aims to keep inflation at a target rate of 2%.However, official figures released on Wednesday showed the Consumer Prices Index (CPI) measure of inflation had risen to 3.1% in August from 2.9% in July, pushing it to its highest rate in six months.The acceleration was driven by rises in the cost of petrol, diesel and airfares. Economists expect that higher global energy costs will feed through to food and fuel prices paid by consumers, meaning the inflation rate is yet to peak.The MPC will be aware that, citing the Middle East conflict and warning inflation was "set to remain well above" its 2% target for some time, the European Central Bank recently raised interest rates to 2.5%.In addition, the US Federal Reserve raised its interest rate to 3.5%-3.75% for similar reasons on Wednesday.However, MPC members will also be keen not to put pressure on employers and further lower the prospects for those seeking a job.Households feel the impact of a rising Bank rate through higher borrowing costs, but can benefit from more generous savings rates.Given the global picture, and market expectations of a higher Bank rate, a host of major lenders have already increased the cost of new fixed-rate mortgages in recent days.Andrew Montlake, chief executive of mortgage broker Coreco, said that the latest data showed that "the inflation dragon has not been fully slain"."If inflation proves sticky, lenders' funding costs stay under pressure, which makes cheaper mortgages harder to deliver," he said."We are already seeing lenders reprice upwards, so this will do little to calm things down. Borrowers should not panic, but anyone approaching the end of a fixed rate should start looking early, secure an option and keep reviewing it."The average two-year fixed residential mortgage rate is at its highest since 11 May, at 5.77%, while the average five-year is at its highest since 8 November 2023, at 5.83%, according to financial information service Moneyfacts.Savers may be offered more generous returns, but the spending power of their savings could be eroded by the rising cost of living."It's almost impossible to time things just right, so I would urge households to focus on what's best for them now, in the medium term and in the longer term," said Harriet Guevara, chief savings officer at Nottingham Building Society."For savers, regularly check that your savings are earning a competitive return and that you have the right balance between easy access and money you can afford to put away for longer."

schema.headline: Interest rates hold expected but Bank of England facing tough choices

title: New hope for breast cancer patients as life-extending drug now on NHS in England
description: Patients in England with a specific type of incurable breast cancer can now access a life-extending drug on the NHS, two years after it was deemed too
body: Patients in England with a specific type of incurable breast cancer can now access a life-extending drug on the NHS, two years after it was deemed too expensive by a health body.  Enhertu can give patients almost seven extra months to live on average - with some living up to three years longer.Women in Scotland have had access to the drug on the NHS since 2023, and it is available in 26 other European countries.Charities and patients have campaigned for it to be more widely available since 2024, when the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) said Enhertu was not good value for money.From Thursday, doctors in England are now able to prescribe it, with Wales expected to follow shortly but the guidance doesn't automatically apply to Northern Ireland.Health Secretary Yvette Cooper said: "Enhertu can be life-changing, and this recommendation means NHS patients will finally be able to benefit from it."It is a tribute to the campaigners and charities who never stopped pressing for this."This decision will affect about 1,000 women a year with a specific type of breast cancer, HER2-low.Charity Breast Cancer Now said that while campaigners' "persistence paid off", thousands of people have missed out on access to Enhertu and many have died.The charity's chief executive, Claire Rowney, said: "Today we can finally say we did it." However, she adds that "we can't celebrate this momentous decision without remembering the devastating cost of this delay".Kate Wills, 51, understands this mix of emotions. She has HER2-low metastatic breast cancer, which has spread to her bones and lungs. But nothing about her suggests that she is terminally ill.She has a high-powered job and is a wife and mum. Her social media feed shows a full and happy life - only the occasional medical appointment hints all is not well.Kate says it has been "incredibly painful" to know that Enhertu could keep her alive for longer but she couldn't get it.The BBC understands that the drug companies Daiichi Sankyo and AstraZeneca have not substantially lowered their prices since the drug was first rejected.The reason NICE has reversed its decision is largely because of a trade deal with the USA, where the UK government agreed to spend 25% more on medicines.As part of this, NICE has increased how much the NHS will pay for every extra year of good quality life a medication can give.This is known as a QALY (Quality-Adjusted Life Year) - and the upper threshold per QALY has gone from £30,000 to £35,000.At the end of August, NICE also introduced a different, more nuanced, way of measuring a patient's quality of life. These two changes were enough to tip the balance.It is thought that patient campaigns for Enhertu - and other drugs - have helped too.Daiichi Sankyo and AstraZeneca welcome NICE's decision, but the latter is calling for "strong collaboration" across the healthcare system to ensure "faster, more equitable patient access in the future".Breast Cancer Now's Claire Rowney says: "We are calling on the government, NICE, NHS England and the pharmaceutical industry to work together to fix this broken system, so that people with incurable metastatic breast cancer are not forced to spend precious months and years campaigning for treatments that could give them more time."Helen Knight, director of medicines evaluation at NICE, says she is pleased a "commercial solution" means the treatment can be made available on the NHS in England but adds she knows the decision "comes too late for many families"."Our role is important in ensuring NHS spending on new medicines reflects the benefits they deliver while protecting valuable health resources for other essential patient services," she says.For Kate, the thought of dying before she had to, "when there was a drug that I just could almost reach but couldn't get", was "so incredibly painful"."To know that I can get it now is absolutely everything."

schema.headline: New hope for breast cancer patients as life-extending drug now on NHS in England

title: Body found in search for missing Suffolk boy Noah Woods, 3
description: Image source, Family handoutImage caption, Noah Woods was described as looking "happy and healthy" by one of the last people to see himByShivani Chaud
body: Image source, Family handoutImage caption, Noah Woods was described as looking "happy and healthy" by one of the last people to see himByShivani Chaudhari and Lewis AdamsA body has been found in the search for missing three-year-old boy Noah Woods, police have confirmed.Noah disappeared at about 15:00 BST on Tuesday from a playground in Brantham, Suffolk, after becoming separated from a relative.Supt Tom Pearse of Suffolk Police said dive teams recovered the body of a child from a nearby pond.He said the death was being treated as unexplained but not suspicious.Figure caption, CCTV footage shows the last sighting of Noah at the playgroundSupt Pearse said formal identification had yet to take place, but Noah's family had been informed. "Our thoughts are with Noah's family and all those who knew him," he said."We have been overwhelmed by the outpouring of public support and people putting on their boots to help."Police said at least 1,300 members of the public had helped in the search for the missing boy, who was non-verbal and partially deaf.People from as far afield as Birmingham and Hampshire had turned up to help.Helicopters, dog units and members of the public had been scouring the area, close to the estuary of the River Stour on the Essex border.Volunteer efforts had been co-ordinated from Brantham Leisure Centre and the village hall, which ran out of hi-vis vests due to the number of volunteers.Those looking for Noah had been told he would not respond to shouting.Image source, PA ImagesImage caption, Supt Tom Pearse of Suffolk Police said: "Our thoughts are with Noah's family and all those who knew him"Michael Crowley, who was working opposite the playground on Tuesday and was one of the last people to see Noah before he went missing, said: "He looked happy and healthy as anything."Jessica Gammons, a mother-of-two from Kelvedon, in Essex, was among the many volunteers who went out to look for the toddler.She said she felt compelled join the search, despite being heavily pregnant, because her son, like Noah, is three years old."I kept thinking to myself 'If this was my son, I'd want everyone possible to help,'" she said."It's such a sad situation. I can't stop thinking about him."Image source, Charlie Jones/BBCImage caption, Jessica Gammons, a mother of two, was among the volunteers who helped in the searchSearches had widened to include East Bergholt and Manningtree, over the Essex border, on Wednesday.Divers from the Metropolitan Police were called in to search Decoy Pond, a nearby fishing lake.The pond is about 350 yds (320m) away from the playground where Noah was last seen.Image source, PA MediaImage caption, Police said at least 1,300 members of the public had joined emergency services in the search for the missing boyImage source, GoogleSupt Pearse continued: "Since Noah was reported as missing, a vast number of our officers and staff have been deployed in numerous functions in the search for Noah and support for his family."We've been supported by Suffolk HART (Hazardous Area Response Team), SULSAR (Suffolk Lowland Search and Rescue), Environment Agency, HM Coastguard, Fire and Rescue Service and the ambulance service.  "As a parent myself, I completely understand why people would want to help and such a response is one that typifies the strong sense of community and the heart-warming nature of Suffolk people that make the county such a special place. "I am sure you appreciate the family now need time, space and privacy and I thank you for your understanding in this."

schema.headline: Body found in search for missing Suffolk boy Noah Woods, 3

title: US interest rates raised for first time in three years
description: US interest rates have been raised for the first time in more than three years and could be increased further in a bid to slow rising prices.Rates wer
body: US interest rates have been raised for the first time in more than three years and could be increased further in a bid to slow rising prices.Rates were hiked to 3.75%-4% from 3.5%-3.75% by the Federal Reserve in a unanimous decision, despite fierce opposition from President Donald Trump, who had called for rates to be cut.Fed Chair Kevin Warsh said the move was because "inflation is too high and has been for too long", adding that it was a "sober" and "responsible decision".After the announcement, Trump expressed support for Warsh but said the Fed board, which votes on rate decisions, was "hostile".Higher interest rates make borrowing more expensive for people wanting to secure loans, mortgages, and credit cards, but can lead to better returns on savings.Warsh said during a press conference on Wednesday following the decision that, while there was "an attitude of optimism" within the Fed leadership, inflation remained a problem.Like many central banks, the Fed has a target of keeping inflation at 2% or below. Warsh noted that US inflation has been above the target "for more than five years".That has helped make affordability one of the top concerns of American voters, who have seen fuel prices surge in response to soaring wholesale oil prices since the start of the US-Israel war with Iran. This has driven up the cost of many goods and services, as well.While the Fed "cannot affect any individual price – whether it be oil prices, whether it be food stuffs at the grocery store", Warsh said, the central bank can work to keep  price rises from broadening across the economy.He added that strength in the jobs market and wider economy meant the Fed was staying focused on stabilising prices, and that those least well off had the most to gain from lower inflation.Central banks tend to increase rates when inflation is high to discourage spending and encourage saving, in the hope this will reduce the pace of price rises. But it's a balancing act, as higher rates can also encourage businesses to hold off on investing and hurt economic growth.When he was confirmed, Democratic lawmakers had said Warsh would be Trump's "sock puppet" and many Fed watchers expected him to carry out Trump's persistent demands to slash rates. Trump had been heavily critical of Warsh's predecessor Jerome Powell for not cutting them.Asked on Wednesday about the message the rate hike sent to Trump, Warsh chuckled before saying: "I have got nothing for you on a discussion with the president."Trump told reporters later "I'm relying on Kevin [Warsh], but he's got, you know, a very tough board"."And the, interest rates are too high. They're not appropriate... I talked to Kevin and I said, 'you might as well vote with the board because it's not going to matter.' The board is very hostile, they're very political," he added.Earlier, Trump said on social media: "LOWER THE INTEREST RATES FOR THE UNITED STATES OF AMERICA, AND FAST!"Democrats on Capitol Hill said the rate increase would make loans costlier and, in turn, more Americans would go into debt."This is going to make everything become more expensive," said Chuck Schumer, the top Democrat in the Senate. "This is because Donald Trump does not know how to manage the economy."The Fed's hike is the first rate move in any direction since they were cut in December 2025. The last time they were raised was in July 2023. The increase could help push up mortgage rates for home buyers and lead to Americans paying more on other types of debt.Major US banks JP Morgan, KeyCorp, and BNY all raised their prime lending rate on Wednesday to 7% from 6.75%, which will affect rates charged on credit cards and personal loans.Mortgage costs have climbed over the past year but remain below peaks seen in 2023. A 30-year fixed deal is 6.76% on average, while a 15-year deal is 6.09%, according to figures from Freddie Mac.Many US homeowners have 30-year and 15-year fixed-rate mortgages, and changes to interest rates will not impact their monthly repayments. But higher rates could affect those looking to secure a new mortgage or refinance.Warsh declined to provide his own view on where he saw the Fed's rates going, but the majority of his fellow policymakers said they believe rates would be hiked again before the end of this year to between 4-4.25%. A small majority also said rates could rise further to the 4.25-4.5% next year, before cuts begin in 2028 and 2029. The forecast suggested price rises will ease in the coming years, with inflation, the measure used to assess the cost of living, predicted to fall steadily to the Fed's target by 2029.The US Fed is not alone in facing rising inflation since the Iran war, with the European Central Bank raising rates last week and the Bank of England set to make its own decision on Thursday.

schema.headline: US interest rates raised for first time in three years

title: Chelsea: Clearlake Capital acquires full control as Todd Boehly, Mark Walter and Hansjorg Wyss sell stakes
description: Chelsea chairman Todd Boehly and director Mark Walter have sold their stakes in the club to majority owner Clearlake Capital.Swiss billionaire Hansjor
body: Chelsea chairman Todd Boehly and director Mark Walter have sold their stakes in the club to majority owner Clearlake Capital.Swiss billionaire Hansjorg Wyss has also sold his stake, meaning Clearlake - led by co-founders Behdad Eghbali and Jose E. Feliciano - have now acquired full control of the club.Boehly, Walter and Wyss each had a 12.8% stake, with Clearlake previously owning 61.5% of the Blues.American Boehly will leave his role as chairman, a position he has held since 2022, when the consortium bought the club for £2.3bn from Roman Abramovich, who was sanctioned by the UK government in March 2022 over alleged links to Russian president Vladimir Putin - something he has denied.BBC Sport reported in August that Boehly and Walter were exploring selling their stakes.Multiple sources said talks started within Chelsea's ownership group after a rift, first apparent in 2024, led both sides to explore buying each other out.Boehly, who is a co-owner of baseball franchise the Los Angeles Dodgers, said it had been an "honour" to serve as Chelsea chairman."I would like to thank the many who helped secure a bright future for the club, including the English Premier League, the coaches and players, the talented leadership and staff at Chelsea, and the legions of dedicated fans," he added."I have valued my partnership with Clearlake and the wider ownership group, and the collective decisions and investment we have made to support the immediate and long-term success of the club. I am confident that Chelsea is well positioned for continued success under Clearlake's leadership."Since the takeover in 2022, Chelsea's highest Premier League finish is fourth in 2024-25, with the club also winning the Uefa Conference League and Fifa Club World Cup that season.The club have also had a remarkably high turnover of players over the past four years, with the initial strategy focusing on signing young players to long-term contracts.Chelsea finished 10th in the Premier League last season and appointed Xabi Alonso as their manager in the summer.Eghbali and Feliciano thanked Boehly for his "time and contribution" as chairman, saying he will "always be a part of the Chelsea story and family".They added their focus is to "continue investing in the club's infrastructure, sporting performance, player development and delivering long-term success for Chelsea and the club's supporters".Chelsea have ongoing plans either to redevelop Stamford Bridge or move to a new stadium, which sources say had created tension at times between Boehly's camp and Clearlake.A club statement said there will be "no changes to the day-to-day operations, leadership or strategy at the club" as a result of Clearlake assuming full control.Walter, the co-owner and chief executive of global finance firm Guggenheim Partners, where Boehly also began his financial career, last month sold the Los Angeles Lakers for a record $12.5bn (£9.23bn) - a year after buying a majority stake in the NBA franchise.Separately, US federal prosecutors and the Securities and Exchange Commission are investigating companies in Walter's business empire.

schema.headline: Chelsea: Clearlake Capital acquires full control as Todd Boehly, Mark Walter and Hansjorg Wyss sell stakes
